column18:
To improve the morale of soldiers within my company or battalion, I would focus on three key areas: leadership engagement, professional development, and soldier welfare.

Leadership Engagement – Strong leadership is the foundation of high morale. I would ensure that leaders at all levels are actively engaged with their soldiers, fostering an environment of trust and open communication. Regular check-ins, town hall meetings, and anonymous feedback channels would help identify concerns early and address them effectively.

Professional Development – Soldiers need to feel that their careers are progressing. I would advocate for increased training opportunities, MOS-specific certifications, and leadership development programs. Additionally, I would work with retention and R&R teams to ensure soldiers have clear paths to reclassify into MOSs that align with their skills and career goals if they choose to extend their service.

Soldier Welfare – Ensuring soldiers' well-being directly impacts morale. I would push for improvements in work-life balance by enforcing reasonable duty schedules, increasing access to mental health resources, and recognizing outstanding performance through awards and incentives. Additionally, team-building activities, mentorship programs, and unit events would strengthen cohesion and unit pride.

column17: The Virginia national guard has increasingly become a less serious organization where standards are consistently not upheld. Discipline within the ranks has collapsed, and the termination of physical punishment has exacerbated this issue.  Many times there will be zero consequences for soldiers who fail to maintain the standard.  The standard meaning attending drill, passing the ACFT, and general MOS competence. These issues combined drain the motivated solider of any desire to continue to serve.  A secondary issue would be the overuse of the national guard.  Many soldiers were promised the time commitment of a weekend a month, and two weeks in the summer.  After an extended period within the National Guard including a deployment, I have yet to ever enjoy the training schedule that was promised to me. It is difficult to age, develop a career, earn a living, and live a life, when the national guard continues to increase its time commitment. There are those who wish to continue to serve, but serving more than a month per year proves difficult. It is difficult to explain to one’s employer that they will be missing work for annual trainings that last 4 weeks.

column16: Over time, some leadership positions aren’t being filled by those who prioritize developing and supporting junior soldiers. Certain NCOs in different sections don’t always take the time to listen or understand the challenges younger soldiers face, which can lead to frustration and a lack of motivation to stay in. When leadership isn’t fully engaged in mentorship and professional growth, it impacts overall morale and career progression.
column17:
I am not interested in extending or re-enlisting because I am mentally and physically exhausted from my time in the military. The process of getting promoted was unnecessarily difficult and took a significant toll on my mental well-being. It often felt like no matter how much effort I put in, the system was working against me, making it hard to stay motivated.

Additionally, I’ve lost confidence in leadership due to repeated instances where I was told, ‘I’ll check into it,’ only for there to be no follow-up or action. This pattern of empty promises and lack of accountability made me feel undervalued and unheard. Over time, the combination of these experiences drained my passion for continuing my service. I’ve reached a point where I need to prioritize my mental and physical health, and I believe it’s in my best interest to move on to the next chapter of my life outside of the military.
column18:
To improve morale within the company or battalion, leadership needs to be more engaged, accountable, and proactive in supporting soldiers. One of the biggest frustrations I’ve experienced is the lack of follow-through when soldiers bring up concerns or career development questions. If leaders commit to checking into something, they need to actually follow up and take action. This would help rebuild trust and show that soldiers’ voices matter.

Additionally, the promotion process should be more transparent and fair. Too often, it feels like a confusing, discouraging battle, which leads to frustration and burnout. Clearer guidance, mentorship, and advocacy from leadership would make a huge difference in keeping soldiers motivated and invested in their careers.

Finally, I would encourage leaders to take the time to actually listen to junior soldiers. Too many NCOs dismiss concerns without truly understanding the challenges younger soldiers face. Creating a culture where feedback is valued and acted upon would go a long way in improving morale and retention
